title: Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless v. Barry
lead: Families seek fair procedures for scarce emergency shelter while advocates challenge limited waiting-room access; the appeal separates those two rights.

actors.name: Washington Legal Clinic, staff, a private shelter, and homeless mothers
actors.role: Plaintiffs challenging shelter administration and advocate-access limits.

actors.name: District of Columbia officials
actors.role: Defendants defending allocation discretion and waiting-room restrictions.

actors.name: Unsolicited advocates
actors.role: People offering assistance without an existing client in the shelter office.

proceedings: The District Court found a shelter property interest and ordered administrative improvements; it also invalidated the weekly advocate schedule.
The District appealed those rulings, while the adverse equal-protection judgment was not appealed by plaintiffs.
The D.C. Circuit reversed the property ruling and remanded, affirmed the access ruling, and declined the inadequately presented funding issue.
limits: Shelters were full; this was not a demand for new beds or a dispute over vacant beds withheld for paperwork. The court did not review the adverse equal-protection judgment or decide the merits of the cursory funding argument.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The District changes its shelter statutes and allocation practices
sections.cue: What remained mandatory after the entitlement disclaimers?
paragraphs: A 1984 initiative guaranteed adequate overnight shelter, and a 1987 law created a temporary program for eligible homeless families and required pursuit of available federal funding. Following costly litigation, the Council amended both in 1990 to disclaim individual or family entitlements. Objective eligibility criteria nevertheless remained, including homelessness, applicable payment or service, restrictions concerning prior shelter use, taxes, expulsions or evictions, and reasonably available supporting documents.

No law specified allocation among eligible families when shelter was scarce. Under the initial daily first-come system, families camped outside and unsuccessful eligible families restarted the next day; some never obtained shelter. An early-1994 waiting list assigned numbers and document checklists and required daily calls. Numbers generally came up one or two months later, by which time roughly half had dropped out. Final eligibility was then assessed; eligible families remaining eventually received shelter. Available family spaces fell from 495 in late 1994 to 139 in May 1995.

sources.pinpoint: Statutes and practices; Majority; 107 F.3d at 33–34,36–37

sections.title: The Clinic challenges paperwork, delay, and restricted access
sections.cue: Which separate rulings reached the appeal?
paragraphs: In 1993 the Clinic, staff, a private shelter, and mothers alleged burdensome documentation, slow hearings, and statutory and constitutional violations. They also challenged access for unsolicited advocates, limited to Wednesday mornings and Tuesday and Friday afternoons, one at a time. Advocates with clients could enter whenever the office opened.

The District withdrew from federal emergency assistance shortly before a preliminary hearing, mooting that request. Plaintiffs added a claim concerning the then-mandatory participation duty. Although later emergency legislation made participation discretionary, the District Court declared violation from July 1, 1993 through April 11, 1995.

It recognized a shelter property interest and, after trial, required clearer document standards, better office coordination, and quicker appeals. It treated the waiting room as a nonpublic forum, upheld the one-advocate limit, but invalidated the weekly schedule. Only the District appealed due process and access; plaintiffs did not appeal their equal-protection loss.

sections.title: The majority separates eligibility from an entitlement to scarce shelter
sections.cue: Why did the current waiting list not bind future allocation choices?
paragraphs: Tatel, joined by Ginsburg, applied Roth’s requirement of a legitimate entitlement under an independent legal source. Unlike Goldberg’s entitlement for everyone satisfying welfare criteria, eligibility here did not compel a benefit for every qualifying family. Scarcity combined with unrestricted allocation choice mattered.

The office could change from its current waiting list to daily priority, infant or disability preferences, or a rolling pool, potentially leaving some eligible families unserved. Review procedures could correct eligibility errors, as the Clinic often achieved, without limiting allocation discretion.

Administrative understandings can sometimes create property, but not an entitlement contrary to legislative intent. The majority doubted that a bare disclaimer could defeat an otherwise unequivocal grant; here it reinforced an operative scheme preserving discretion. It reserved unalleged special reliance or contractual circumstances and did not make every statutory disclaimer automatically conclusive.

sections.title: Wald sees a conditional claim under the existing allocation system
sections.cue: What relief did her partial dissent favor?
paragraphs: Wald regarded the interest as contingent, not absent. Traditional property permits future interests that may never vest, and power to change a program does not eliminate protection while it operates. Priority setting differed from arbitrary refusal when an eligible family reached available shelter under current practice.

Detailed notice, hearing, evidence, and review rules constrained officials; Perry supported settled institutional expectations. At minimum, an eligible family at the head of the list when a unit opened had a protected claim. She read the disclaimer as denying a demand for enough funding for everyone, not permitting arbitrary distribution of existing resources, and would preserve the documentation and appeal remedies. She did not demand shelter on request or judicial funding increases.

sources.pinpoint: Wald partial dissent; 107 F.3d at 39–46 & nn.1–12

sections.title: The advocate schedule fails reasonableness review
sections.cue: What is the appeal’s precise mixed result?
paragraphs: Accepting the unchallenged nonpublic-forum classification, the court found the weekly schedule unreasonable. The one-person limit already addressed crowding, vulnerability to solicitation did not change by time slot, and actual nonenforcement weakened the stated concerns. Other forums’ financial-solicitation bans did not justify these limits on offers of help. The one-at-a-time rule remained.

The District put its request to vacate the funding declaration only in a cursory closing footnote, omitted it from issues, and did not pursue it in reply. The court declined that inadequately presented question without deciding withdrawal’s merits.

The court reversed the property ruling and remanded, affirmed invalidation of the access schedule, and left the funding argument unresolved. Wald dissented only on property and due process, making that issue two to one without dissent on access.

sources.pinpoint: Access and funding; Final judgment; 107 F.3d at 38–39
